opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think data filtering is one of those ideas that sounds really clean when you first hear it. If you don't want the model to know how to do X, just don't show it X during training. And to be clear, I think it's worth doing. It's one of the few interventions where you're actually changing what the model *is*, rather than training it to refuse after the fact, which we know is pretty brittle.

But there are a few limitations I keep coming back to.

The first is that it's really hard to define the boundary of "the dangerous stuff." Knowledge isn't neatly partitioned. If you want to remove, say, detailed knowledge about synthesizing some dangerous compound, the relevant information is spread across organic chemistry textbooks, lab safety manuals, patents, forum posts, and papers that are mostly about something else. You can remove the obviously bad documents, but the long tail is enormous. Your classifier has to be both very precise and have very high recall at the scale of trillions of tokens, and that's a hard combination.

The second is that models are good at putting things together. Even if no single document contains the dangerous thing, the model might learn enough adjacent pieces to reconstruct it. Generalization is the whole point of these systems, so you're fighting against the thing that makes them useful. The more capable the model gets, the less you need to show it directly.

Third, there's a real cost to legitimate uses. A lot of dangerous knowledge is dual-use. The biology that helps someone do harm is often the same biology a vaccine researcher or a doctor needs. Filter aggressively and you degrade the model for a lot of people doing good work. Filter conservatively and you haven't removed much.

Fourth, and this one matters a lot from a security perspective, filtering only helps against the knowledge the model learns in pretraining. It doesn't help with what someone supplies at inference time. If the model is a strong reasoner and can read documents or search the web, an adversary can just hand it the missing pieces in context. Same with fine-tuning on open-weight models: if someone has the weights, they can teach the missing knowledge back, and it may take surprisingly little data because the model already has all the surrounding scaffolding.

And finally, it's hard to verify. How do you know the filtering worked? You can run evals, but absence of evidence on your eval isn't strong evidence the capability isn't there. People keep finding that capabilities they thought were removed can be elicited with the right prompting or a small amount of fine-tuning.

So my overall take is: it's a useful layer, probably more robust than refusal training alone, and I'd like to see more of it. But it's not a guarantee, and I'd be worried if people treated "we filtered the training data" as the end of the safety story rather than one piece of it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that it's a reasonable idea, and I understand why people want to do it. If you don't want the model to be able to tell you how to synthesize some dangerous compound, the most obvious thing to do is just not put that in the training data. And at some level that has to help. But I think there are a bunch of limitations, and I'd put them roughly into three buckets.

The first is that it's really hard to actually exclude things. The internet is enormous, and the thing you're trying to remove doesn't come neatly labeled. The dangerous chemistry information isn't just in a textbook chapter called "how to make dangerous things." It's spread across patents, academic papers, forum posts, Wikipedia articles about historical incidents, safety data sheets that tell you what not to do, which is of course exactly the same information read backwards. So you build a classifier to filter it out, and the classifier has false negatives, and some fraction of the content gets through. And then the question becomes whether a small fraction is enough. And for a lot of this knowledge, the answer is probably yes. You don't need ten thousand copies of a fact for the model to learn it. You need one, or a handful.

The second bucket is that the capability isn't really the fact. These models are good at putting things together. If I remove every document that says "A plus B gives you C," but I leave in the documents that explain what A does and what B does and the general chemistry of how these reactions work, a sufficiently capable model may just figure out C. That's the whole point of the thing, right? We want models that can reason from general principles to specific conclusions. So excluding specific conclusions from the training data is somewhat at odds with the thing you're trying to build. The better the model gets, the less this kind of filtering buys you, because the model needs fewer and fewer of the dots to connect them.

And the third bucket is more about the dual-use problem. A lot of the information you'd want to exclude is the same information that someone legitimate needs. The person doing biosecurity research needs to understand how pathogens work. The person who writes antivirus software needs to understand how malware works. I come from a security background, so this is the one I think about most. If you remove all the information about how exploits work, you've made the model worse at finding vulnerabilities, worse at explaining why some piece of code is dangerous, worse at helping defenders. And the people who already have the knowledge, the ones you're actually worried about, aren't the ones who were going to learn it from the model anyway. So there's a real cost, and it's not obvious the benefit outweighs it in every case.

There's also a more subtle point, which is that if you train on filtered data and then the model gets fine-tuned later, or someone does something at inference time to elicit the knowledge, you don't actually have a strong guarantee about what's in there. You have a guarantee about what you tried to remove. Those are different things. And a lot of my work has been about showing that these two things are different, that the model knows things you didn't think it knew, or memorized things you didn't think it memorized.

So I don't think data exclusion is useless. For some narrow categories where the information really is concentrated in a small number of identifiable sources, it probably does something. But I'm skeptical of treating it as a primary safety mechanism. It's more of a thing you do in addition to other things, and you should be honest that it's leaky, that it degrades as models get more capable, and that you probably can't measure very well how much it's actually helping.

astra-6.text:
I think the fundamental limitation is that removing information from the training data doesn’t necessarily prevent the model from figuring it out. There’s a difference between not knowing a particular fact and not being able to derive that fact from other things you know.

Suppose you want a model to be useful for chemistry, but you don’t want it to help someone make a dangerous substance. You could remove documents that explicitly describe how to make that substance. But a sufficiently capable model might still work out a synthesis from the general chemistry you’ve left in. Those same underlying principles are useful for perfectly legitimate tasks.

That doesn’t mean filtering is useless. It can make certain information harder to obtain. But I wouldn’t treat the absence of an explicit recipe in the training data as a guarantee that the model can’t produce one. As models become more capable of reasoning, you have to worry about what they can infer, not just what they’ve seen.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest limitation is that information isn’t neatly separable. If you want a model to be good at biology, for example, a lot of the knowledge that makes it useful for legitimate research might also be useful to someone trying to do something harmful. You can remove documents that explicitly describe the harmful thing, but that doesn’t necessarily remove the ability to figure it out from the pieces that remain.

And that becomes more important as models get better at reasoning. You don’t need to have seen the exact answer during training if you can derive it from other things you know. So filtering training data can help reduce some risks, but I wouldn’t treat it as a guarantee that a model can’t acquire or reconstruct a particular capability.
